title: Mishnah, Gemara, Rashi, Tosafot: The Vilna Page
bigQuestion: How does one printed page hold a conversation that lasted more than a thousand years?

story.title: The Printer of Venice
story.kicker: A Christian printer in Venice decides where every commentary will sit, and the choice lasts five hundred years.
paragraphs: Venice, around 1520. Daniel Bomberg is not Jewish. He came from Antwerp, in what is now Belgium, and he prints books for a living. Printing is still a new craft. Most books in the world are still copied by hand. Bomberg has a plan that no one has finished before: print the whole Babylonian Talmud, every tractate, in one matching set.

The problem is not only the size of the text. The problem is what to put around it. For hundreds of years, Jewish students had read the Talmud with two companions. One was Rashi, a teacher from France who died in 1105. The other was the Tosafot, notes by Rashi's grandsons and their students. Handwritten copies often put these notes in the margins. Every copy did it a little differently.

Bomberg's Jewish editors and typesetters work out a design. The Mishnah and Gemara go in the middle of the page, in a large square block. Rashi's comments go in a narrow column on the inner side, next to the binding. The Tosafot go in a column on the outer side. All three columns start and end together, so the page looks like a frame around a window.

The shop also numbers the pages. Each leaf gets one number, and each leaf has two sides, a and b. Berakhot 2a means the front of the second leaf of tractate Berakhot. The first leaf is the title page, so the text begins on 2a. Almost every printing since then has kept the same page numbers, so a student in Chicago and a student in Jerusalem can open to the very same words.

Historians note that Bomberg had the pope's permission to print and that his editors included Jews and converts. His set was finished by about 1523. Later printers copied his layout. When the Romm family of Vilna printed their famous edition in the 1880s, they kept the frame, kept the numbers, and added more notes around the edges. The page you meet in this chapter is, in a real sense, Bomberg's page.
story.think: Why might it matter that every printed Talmud keeps the same page numbers? Who is helped by that choice?

lessons.title: The Center of the Page
lessons.mainIdea: The middle of a Talmud page holds the Mishnah and the Gemara, the two oldest layers of the text.
reading: Open any tractate of the Babylonian Talmud and look at the middle of the page. You will see a large block of Hebrew letters. This block holds two texts, one inside the other. The older one is the *Mishnah*, a law code that rabbinic tradition says Judah the Prince arranged around the year 200. The newer one is the *Gemara*, the record of how later rabbis discussed each Mishnah.

The two are not separated by color or by a different typeface. Instead, the word Mishnah, or a shortened form of it, marks where a Mishnah begins. The word Gemara marks where the discussion starts. A short paragraph of Mishnah can be followed by pages of Gemara. Sometimes a single Mishnah gets only a few lines.

Readers of the Talmud usually call the two layers together the *Talmud*. Scholars point out that the Mishnah is written mostly in Hebrew, while the Gemara is written mostly in Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Babylonia. So the center of the page is already a conversation between two centuries and two languages.

words.d: the early rabbinic law code, arranged around the year 200 according to tradition, written mostly in Hebrew
the recorded discussion of the Mishnah by later rabbis, written mostly in Aramaic
the Mishnah and the Gemara together; the Babylonian Talmud is the larger of the two Talmuds

look.title: Two Layers, One Block
look.text: Picture a page where the middle block begins with a short law: the time for saying the evening Shema starts when the priests come in to eat their portion. Right after it, without a new heading, a new voice asks why the law starts with the evening and not the morning. The first voice is the Mishnah. The second is the Gemara.
look.prompt: How could you tell, just from the way the two voices talk, which one is the older text and which is the commentary on it?

check.q: Which two texts share the center block of a Talmud page?
check.why: The center block holds the Mishnah, the older law code, and the Gemara, the later discussion of it.

check.q: In what language is most of the Gemara written?
check.why: Scholars note that the Gemara is written mostly in Aramaic, the spoken language of Jews in Babylonia. The Mishnah is mostly Hebrew.

check.q: According to rabbinic tradition, who arranged the Mishnah?
check.why: Tradition holds that Judah the Prince arranged the Mishnah around the year 200. Rav Ashi is linked to the Gemara, and Rashi and Bomberg came much later.

lessons.title: Rashi on the Inside
lessons.mainIdea: Rashi's commentary sits on the inner margin and explains the words and the flow of the Gemara.
reading: Next to the binding, in a narrow column, sits the commentary of *Rashi*. Rashi is a short name made from the letters of Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki. He lived in Troyes, in northern France, from 1040 to 1105. He earned his living, according to later accounts, from wine. He wrote a commentary on almost the whole Babylonian Talmud.

Rashi's comments are short. He picks a word or phrase from the Gemara, repeats it, and then explains it in a few words. He tells you who is speaking, what a hard Aramaic word means, and what the question is really asking. Students for centuries have said that without Rashi the page would be locked.

The letters in Rashi's column look different from the letters in the center. Printers used a rounder, semi-cursive typeface for commentaries, and it became known as Rashi script. Historians point out that Rashi himself never wrote in this script. It is named after him only because his commentary was the first famous text printed in it.

words.d: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki (1040–1105) of Troyes, France, whose short commentary sits on the inner margin of the Talmud page
a semi-cursive Hebrew typeface used for commentaries; named for Rashi's commentary, not for his handwriting

look.title: A Word and Its Gloss
look.text: Imagine a line of Gemara that says a certain rabbi 'went out to the courtyard.' Beside it, Rashi's column repeats the words 'to the courtyard' and adds: the place where the students waited, outside the study hall. That is the whole comment. It does not argue. It tells you what the words mean and where the scene happens.
look.prompt: What kind of help does a comment like this give a reader? Why might a beginner need it more than an expert?

check.q: Where does Rashi's commentary sit on the standard Talmud page?
choices: At the bottom of the page
On the inner margin, next to the binding
check.why: Rashi's column runs along the inner margin. The Tosafot run along the outer margin.

check.q: What does Rashi's commentary mostly do?
choices: Explains words and the flow of the argument
Adds new laws not in the Gemara
check.why: Rashi repeats a phrase from the Gemara and explains what it means and who is speaking, in a few words.

check.q: Why is a certain typeface called Rashi script?
choices: Because Rashi's commentary was the first famous text printed in it
Because Rashi wrote his notes in it by hand
Because it was made in Rashi's town of Troyes
check.why: Historians note that Rashi never wrote in this script. Printers used it for commentaries, and his was the best known.

lessons.title: Tosafot on the Outside
lessons.mainIdea: The Tosafot, on the outer margin, are questions and additions from Rashi's grandsons and their students in the 1100s and 1200s.
reading: On the outer edge of the page sits a second column of commentary called the *Tosafot*. The word means additions. These notes were written in France and Germany during the 1100s and 1200s by a group of scholars, not by one person. Several of them were Rashi's own grandsons, including Rabbeinu Tam and Rashbam.

The Tosafot do something different from Rashi. Rashi explains the page in front of you. The Tosafot compare that page with other pages. A note might begin by quoting Rashi, then ask how his reading fits a passage in another tractate, then offer a new answer. They treat the whole Talmud as one book that must agree with itself.

Because the Tosafot ask hard questions, reading them takes practice. A note often opens with a word from the Gemara in bold, then a question, then two or three possible answers. Students in a *beit midrash*, a study hall, often work through a Tosafot note with a partner, since one reader alone can miss a step.

words.d: additions; notes on the outer margin by Rashi's grandsons and students in the 1100s and 1200s that compare pages across the Talmud
a house of study; the hall where Talmud is studied, often in pairs and out loud
Jacob ben Meir (c. 1100–1171), a grandson of Rashi and a leading writer of the Tosafot

look.title: Rashi Reads a Page, Tosafot Read a Book
look.text: Two readers sit at one page. The first says: this word means a loan, and the rabbi speaking is Rav. The second says: yes, but in tractate Bava Metzia the same rabbi seems to say the opposite about loans, so either that page means something else or this one does. The first reader is doing Rashi's job. The second is doing the Tosafot's job.
look.prompt: Which of the two readers would you want first when you are new to a page? Which one helps you see the Talmud as a whole?

check.q: What does the word Tosafot mean?
check.why: Tosafot means additions. The notes add questions and comparisons to Rashi's commentary.

check.q: How do the Tosafot differ from Rashi?
choices: They translate the page into Aramaic
They were written by one author
They compare the page with passages elsewhere in the Talmud
check.why: Rashi explains the page in front of you. The Tosafot ask how it fits with other pages and offer answers.

check.q: Who wrote the Tosafot?
choices: A group of scholars in France and Germany in the 1100s and 1200s
Judah the Prince and his court
The printers of Vilna in the 1880s
check.why: The Tosafot were written by many scholars, including Rashi's grandsons Rabbeinu Tam and Rashbam, over about two centuries.

lessons.title: The Small Print at the Edges
lessons.mainIdea: Around the three main columns, later printers added short references that link a line to the Bible, to law codes and to other pages.
reading: A standard page carries more than three texts. Around the edges, in very small type, sit helpers added by later editors. One helper points from a line of Gemara to the biblical verse it quotes. Another lists where the same teaching appears elsewhere in the Talmud. A third points to the place in the great medieval law codes where the ruling was settled.

These helpers have names. The list of parallel passages is called Masoret HaShas, the tradition of the Talmud. The pointer to the law codes is called Ein Mishpat, the well of judgment. Editions since Vilna also carry short notes by later rabbis, such as the comments of Rabbi Akiva Eger, printed in the margin.

None of this small print is older than the printing press, and much of it was added in the 1800s. Scholars describe the page as a set of layers laid down over time. The Mishnah is the oldest layer. The Gemara is next. Then Rashi, then the Tosafot, then the printers' helpers. Reading a page well means knowing which layer you are in.

words.d: the marginal list of parallel passages, showing where a teaching appears elsewhere in the Talmud
the marginal pointer from a ruling in the Gemara to its place in the medieval law codes

look.title: Layers of a Standard Page
look.cite: Common scholarly datings; the Gemara's closing is often given as c. 500–600 and is debated
look.prompt: How many centuries separate the oldest layer of the page from the newest? What does that tell you about how the page grew?

check.q: What does the Masoret HaShas do on the page?
choices: Lists where the same teaching appears elsewhere in the Talmud
check.why: Masoret HaShas is the marginal list of parallel passages. Explaining words is Rashi's job.

check.q: Which layer of the page is the oldest?
check.why: The Mishnah is the oldest layer, arranged around 200 by tradition. The Ein Mishpat pointers came with printing.

check.q: When was most of the small print at the edges added?
choices: After the printing press, much of it in the 1800s
check.why: The marginal helpers are printers' and later editors' additions. Many were standardized in the Vilna edition of the 1880s.

lessons.title: Two Languages on One Page
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah is mostly Hebrew and the Gemara mostly Aramaic, so reading the Talmud means moving between two related languages.
reading: The Talmud switches languages without warning. The Mishnah is in Hebrew, the language of the Bible, though a later and simpler Hebrew. The Gemara is mostly in *Aramaic*. Aramaic was the common language across much of the Middle East for centuries. Jews in Babylonia spoke it at home and in the market, so their study was recorded in it.

The two languages are cousins. They share an alphabet and many roots. A reader who knows Hebrew can often guess an Aramaic word, but not always. The Gemara also quotes earlier teachings in Hebrew, so a single line can begin in Aramaic, quote a Hebrew *baraita*, and return to Aramaic. Rashi often marks these shifts.

Scholars note that the Jerusalem Talmud, made in the Land of Israel, uses a different western dialect of Aramaic. The Babylonian Talmud uses an eastern dialect. Readers today learn a short list of common Aramaic words first, such as the words for 'he said,' 'a difficulty,' and 'come and hear.' With those, the page starts to open.

words.d: a language related to Hebrew, spoken widely in the ancient Middle East; the main language of the Gemara
an early rabbinic teaching from the age of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah; the Gemara often quotes one as evidence

look.title: Spot the Switch
look.text: Read this made-up line in English that copies the pattern of the page: 'Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: the teaching says, ONE WHO FINDS A LOST OBJECT MUST ANNOUNCE IT. And why is this so? Come and hear.' The capital letters stand for a Hebrew quotation. The rest stands for Aramaic.
look.prompt: Which part of the line is the older teaching being quoted, and which part is the Gemara talking about it? How can you tell?

check.q: Why is the Gemara mostly in Aramaic?
choices: Aramaic was the everyday language of Jews in Babylonia
Hebrew had been forgotten by then
check.why: The rabbis of Babylonia spoke Aramaic, so their study was recorded in it. Hebrew was still used for prayer and for quoting earlier teachings.

check.q: What is a baraita?
choices: A page number in the Vilna edition
An early rabbinic teaching left out of the Mishnah that the Gemara may quote
A commentary written by Rashi's grandsons
The Aramaic word for a question
check.why: A baraita is a teaching from the Mishnah's era that was not included in the Mishnah. The Gemara cites baraitot as proof.

check.q: How do the two Talmuds differ in language?
choices: One is in Hebrew and one in Greek
They use different dialects of Aramaic, western and eastern
check.why: The Jerusalem Talmud uses a western Aramaic dialect and the Babylonian Talmud an eastern one, scholars note.

lessons.title: Studying Aloud, in Pairs
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition studies the page with a partner, out loud, which is one reason the page keeps so many voices.
reading: The page was built to be argued over, not read silently. In a traditional *beit midrash*, students learn with a *chavruta*, a study partner. One reads a line aloud. The other stops and asks what it means. They check Rashi. They try the Tosafot. They disagree, and then they move on. The room is loud.

A saying in Pirkei Avot, a tractate of the Mishnah, advises a student to get a teacher and acquire a companion. Rabbinic readers have long taken this to mean that Torah is studied with others, not alone. The Gemara itself, in tractate Taanit, praises scholars who sharpen one another, like iron on iron, and warns against studying by oneself.

The page's layout fits this way of learning. A pair can point to the center, then to Rashi's column, then to a Tosafot note, without turning a page. Modern classrooms in Chicago and elsewhere that teach Talmud, whether in day schools or in university courses, often keep the pair method even when the students read in English.

words.d: a study partner; the traditional way of studying Talmud is two people reading and arguing together
Chapters of the Fathers, a tractate of the Mishnah made of short sayings about learning and conduct

look.title: Get a Companion
look.text: In Pirkei Avot, a teacher named Yehoshua ben Perachyah is recorded as saying: make yourself a teacher, acquire for yourself a friend, and judge every person favorably. Rabbinic tradition reads the middle phrase as advice about study: find a partner and learn with them.
look.cite: Mishnah Avot 1:6, paraphrased from Charles Taylor, Sayings of the Jewish Fathers (1877)
look.prompt: Why might a tradition that values argument tell students to acquire a companion rather than to study alone?

check.q: What is a chavruta?
choices: A commentary on the outer margin
check.why: A chavruta is a study partner. The traditional way to read the page is two people, out loud.

check.q: What is Pirkei Avot?
choices: A tractate of the Mishnah made of sayings about learning and conduct
The list of parallel passages in the margin
check.why: Pirkei Avot, Chapters of the Fathers, is a tractate of the Mishnah. It contains sayings such as 'acquire for yourself a friend.'

check.q: How does the layout of the page fit the pair method of study?
choices: It hides the commentaries so pairs must guess
A pair can point to the text, Rashi and Tosafot without turning the page
It gives each partner a separate page
It is printed in two colors
check.why: All three main columns share one page, so partners can move between text and commentaries while they argue.

sections.title: From Manuscript to Print to Screen

lessons.title: Bomberg's Venice Edition
lessons.mainIdea: Daniel Bomberg's Venice printing of 1520–23 fixed the page layout and page numbers that nearly every edition since has followed.
reading: Before printing, every Talmud was a handwritten manuscript. Copies were rare and costly. Scholars note that the Talmud was also attacked: in Paris in 1242, cartloads of manuscripts were burned after a public trial. Very few complete medieval manuscripts survive. The best known is the Munich manuscript, copied in 1342, the only complete handwritten Babylonian Talmud that still exists.

Printing changed everything. *Daniel Bomberg*, a Christian printer from Antwerp working in Venice, produced the first complete printed Babylonian Talmud between about 1520 and 1523. His editors set the Mishnah and Gemara in the center with Rashi inside and Tosafot outside. They gave each leaf a number, and each leaf has a front side, a, and a back side, b.

Later printers, Jewish and Christian, copied Bomberg's layout and his numbering. That is why a citation like Berakhot 2a means the same page in a Venice edition, a Vilna edition and a modern one. Historians call this a rare case where one printer's design became the standard for a whole literature for five centuries.

words.d: a Christian printer from Antwerp whose Venice press produced the first complete printed Babylonian Talmud, c. 1520–23
a leaf of a book with two sides; Talmud citations give the leaf number plus a (front) or b (back)

look.title: Milestones of the Text
look.cite: Dates as given in standard histories of the Talmud's printing and translation
look.prompt: Which milestone changed how many people could own a Talmud? Which changed who could read it?

check.q: What did Bomberg's Venice press produce?
choices: The first complete printed Babylonian Talmud
check.why: Bomberg's Venice press printed the first complete Babylonian Talmud between about 1520 and 1523. The Vilna edition came in the 1880s.

check.q: What does the letter b in 'Berakhot 3b' mean?
check.why: Each leaf, or folio, has a front side, a, and a back side, b. Berakhot 3b is the back of leaf 3.

check.q: Why can a citation like Berakhot 2a be found in any standard edition?
choices: Later printers kept Bomberg's layout and page numbers
Rashi assigned the numbers in the 1000s
Each edition renumbers but uses a lookup table
The Mishnah fixed page numbers around 200
check.why: Bomberg's numbering became the standard, so the same words fall on the same page across editions.

lessons.title: The Vilna Shas
lessons.mainIdea: The Romm press in Vilna printed the edition of 1880–86 that became the standard look of the Talmud page.
reading: In the 1800s the city of Vilna, now Vilnius in Lithuania, was a center of Jewish learning and printing. The Romm family ran a large press there. Between 1880 and 1886 they printed a new edition of the whole Babylonian Talmud. It is known as the *Vilna Shas*. Shas is a short form of the Hebrew words for six orders, the six divisions of the Mishnah.

The Vilna edition kept Bomberg's frame and numbering. It added more commentaries around the edges and at the back of each volume, cleaned up many printing errors, and used clear type. Scholars say its editors gathered readings from manuscripts and earlier printings. It was not the first Talmud, but it became the one that most later editions copied, even photographically.

When people today say 'the Talmud page,' they usually mean the Vilna page. Its look is so fixed that a student who learns one page can find their way around any other. Yet the layout is a printer's choice, not part of the text. Manuscripts before 1500 looked quite different, and digital editions today can look different again.

words.d: the edition of the Babylonian Talmud printed by the Romm press in Vilna in 1880–86, which became the standard page
short for shishah sedarim, the six orders of the Mishnah; a common name for the whole Talmud

look.title: What a Layout Says
look.text: Two editions of the same tractate lie side by side. The old manuscript has the Gemara in one wide column with a few notes squeezed in the margin by hand. The Vilna page has a square of text framed by two even columns and a border of tiny references. The words in the center are the same.
look.prompt: What does the Vilna layout tell a reader about how the text is meant to be studied? What might the manuscript have told its reader?

check.q: What does the word Shas stand for?
choices: The six orders of the Mishnah
check.why: Shas is short for shishah sedarim, six orders, the six divisions of the Mishnah. It is used as a name for the whole Talmud.

check.q: When was the Vilna edition printed?
check.why: The Romm press printed the Vilna Shas between 1880 and 1886. Bomberg's edition was 1520–23 and the Soncino translation 1935–52.

check.q: Which statement about the Vilna page is accurate?
choices: It was the first Talmud ever printed
It was copied by hand in Vilna
It removed Rashi and the Tosafot
Its layout is a printers' choice, not part of the original text
check.why: The Vilna page kept and refined Bomberg's layout. The layout is a design decision; the Mishnah and Gemara are far older than any printing.

lessons.title: Editions and Translations Today
lessons.mainIdea: Modern editions and translations, in print and online, open the page to readers who do not know Hebrew or Aramaic.
reading: For most of history, reading the Talmud meant reading Hebrew and Aramaic. In the 1900s, translations began to change that. The Soncino Press in London published a complete English translation between 1935 and 1952. Earlier, Michael Rodkinson had printed a partial and abridged English version in the United States between 1896 and 1903; scholars treat it with care because it leaves out and reshapes much.

Rabbi Adin Steinsaltz began a Hebrew edition in 1965 that added vowels, punctuation and a running commentary; an English version followed. The Schottenstein edition from ArtScroll, finished in 2005, gives an English translation phrase by phrase, with notes. Each edition makes choices about what to explain, and readers in different communities prefer different ones.

Online, the site *Sefaria*, founded in 2011, offers the Hebrew and Aramaic text with an English translation and links to Rashi, Tosafot and thousands of other texts. Many public schools, colleges and libraries use it because it is free. The Vilna page, the Steinsaltz page and a Sefaria screen all carry the same words. What changes is how much help surrounds them.

words.d: a free online library, founded in 2011, that carries the Talmud with English translation and linked commentaries
the text put into another language; every translation of the Talmud makes choices about meaning
the complete English translation published by the Soncino Press of London, 1935–52

look.title: Bringing the Talmud into English
look.cite: Publication dates from the editions' own front matter and standard reference works
look.prompt: Roughly how many years passed between the first complete English Talmud and a free online one? Who gains from each step?

check.q: Which English translation of the Talmud was the first complete one?
check.why: Soncino published the first complete English Talmud. Rodkinson's earlier version was partial and abridged. The Vilna Shas is in Hebrew and Aramaic.

check.q: What does Sefaria offer that a printed Vilna page does not?
choices: The Mishnah in the center of the page
Clickable links to translations and thousands of related texts
check.why: Sefaria carries the same text and commentaries, but links them online with an English translation. The Vilna page already had Rashi and the numbers.

check.q: Why do scholars treat Rodkinson's translation with care?
choices: It is partial and abridged, leaving out and reshaping much
check.why: Rodkinson's English Talmud is public domain but incomplete and reshaped. It must be checked against the page.

lessons.title: How to Cite a Page
lessons.mainIdea: A Talmud citation names the tractate, the leaf number and the side; a Mishnah citation names the tractate, chapter and mishnah.
reading: A *citation* is the short address of a passage. For the Babylonian Talmud it has three parts: the tractate, the leaf number and the side. Berakhot 2a means tractate Berakhot, leaf 2, front side. Bava Metzia 59b means tractate Bava Metzia, leaf 59, back side. Because every standard edition shares Bomberg's numbering, this address works everywhere.

The Mishnah is cited differently, by chapter and paragraph. Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 means tractate Sanhedrin, chapter 4, mishnah 5. Pirkei Avot is usually cited without the word Mishnah, as Avot 1:14. The Jerusalem Talmud is often cited by chapter and law, or by the page of its Venice printing, and scholars sometimes add the letter y. in front of the tractate name.

Learning to cite well matters in this course. When you write about a passage, give its address so a reader can find the very words. Give the translation you used and its year, since translations differ. A citation is a small act of honesty: it lets someone check you.

words.d: the short address of a passage: tractate, leaf and side for the Talmud; tractate, chapter and mishnah for the Mishnah
one of the books of the Mishnah and Talmud, such as Berakhot or Sanhedrin; the Hebrew word is masekhet

look.title: Read the Address
look.text: Here are four addresses: Shabbat 31a. Mishnah Avot 1:14. Bava Batra 21a. Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5. Two of them point to a leaf of the Babylonian Talmud. Two of them point to a paragraph of the Mishnah.
look.prompt: Sort the four addresses into the two kinds. What clue in each one tells you which kind it is?

check.q: What does 'Bava Metzia 59b' point to?
choices: Chapter 59 of Bava Metzia, verse b
Tractate Bava Metzia, leaf 59, back side
check.why: Talmud citations give tractate, leaf and side. The b marks the back of leaf 59.

check.q: How is the Mishnah cited?
choices: By tractate, chapter and mishnah, such as Sanhedrin 4:5
By leaf and side, such as 4a
By volume and page of the Vilna Shas
By the name of the rabbi speaking
check.why: Mishnah citations use chapter and paragraph numbers, like Sanhedrin 4:5, not leaf numbers.

check.q: Why should a citation also name the translation and its year?
choices: Because the page numbers change in every translation
Because translations differ, and a reader needs to find the same words
Because older translations are always better
check.why: Translations make different choices. Naming the one you used lets a reader check what you read.

lessons.title: The Six Orders and Their Tractates
lessons.mainIdea: The Mishnah is arranged in six orders, and each order holds tractates on related subjects.
reading: The Mishnah has 63 tractates, grouped into six *orders*. Rabbinic tradition names them by topic. Zeraim, Seeds, covers blessings and farming laws. Moed, Appointed Time, covers Shabbat and the festivals. Nashim, Women, covers marriage and vows. Nezikin, Damages, covers property, courts and injury. Kodashim, Holy Things, covers the Temple service. Tohorot, Purities, covers ritual purity.

The Babylonian Gemara does not cover every tractate. It discusses about 37 of the 63, mostly in Moed, Nashim, Nezikin and Kodashim, plus Berakhot from Zeraim and Niddah from Tohorot. Scholars suggest that the Babylonian academies focused on laws that still applied in daily life after the Temple was gone.

The names of tractates are often the first thing a student learns. Berakhot means Blessings. Shabbat is the Sabbath. Bava Metzia, the Middle Gate, is about lost objects, loans and wages. Sanhedrin is about courts. Avot, Fathers, is the tractate of sayings. Knowing the name tells you the subject before you read a word.

words.d: one of the six large divisions of the Mishnah, each on a broad subject; in Hebrew, seder
Damages, the order of the Mishnah about property, injury, courts and business
Blessings, the first tractate of the Mishnah and Talmud, about prayer and blessings

look.title: Tractates in the Six Orders
look.cite: Standard count of 63 tractates in the Mishnah, by order
look.prompt: Which orders do you think the Babylonian Gemara covers most fully, and why might that be?

check.q: How many orders does the Mishnah have?
check.why: The Mishnah has six orders, which together hold 63 tractates.

check.q: Which order holds the laws of Shabbat and the festivals?
check.why: Moed, Appointed Time, is the order about Shabbat and the festivals. Nezikin is about damages and courts.

check.q: Why does the Babylonian Gemara skip many tractates, according to scholars?
choices: The academies focused on laws still practiced after the Temple was gone
Those tractates were lost in the fire of 1242
check.why: Scholars suggest the Babylonian academies studied laws that still applied in daily life, such as Shabbat, marriage and property.

lessons.title: Where the Page Protects Someone
lessons.mainIdea: Even a lesson on layout leads to the Talmud's purpose: rules that protect the worker, the owner of a lost object and the person at risk.
reading: The page is a tool, not the point. The point is the questions the text keeps asking. Take the order Nezikin. Its tractate Bava Metzia opens with two people holding one cloak, each claiming it. The Mishnah rules that they divide it and each swears an oath. The Gemara then spends pages asking why an oath is needed and what happens if one of them is lying.

Further on, the same tractate turns to lost objects. Who must return them? What if the finder cannot tell whose it is? The Mishnah lists objects that a finder may keep and objects that must be announced. Rashi explains the terms. The Tosafot compare the rule with a passage in another tractate. Every layer of the page is working on one question: how do you treat what is not yours?

This course follows two threads through the Talmud, argument and mercy. Argument is how the page moves. Mercy is what many rulings protect: the day laborer waiting for wages, the stranger, the person who might be shamed in public. As you learn the layout, keep asking what each page is trying to protect. That question is the best guide through the frame.

words.d: the Middle Gate, a tractate of Nezikin about lost objects, loans, wages and disputed property
the two threads of this course: how the Gemara reasons, and whom its rulings protect

look.title: Two Hold a Cloak
look.text: The opening Mishnah of Bava Metzia describes two people holding one garment. Each says, I found it, and each says, all of it is mine. The Mishnah rules that each one swears that he owns no less than half, and they divide it.
look.cite: Mishnah Bava Metzia 1:1 (Bava Metzia 2a), paraphrased from the Vilna text; compare Rodkinson, Babylonian Talmud (1896–1903)
look.prompt: Why might the Mishnah require an oath before dividing the cloak? Whom does that rule protect?

check.q: What case opens tractate Bava Metzia?
choices: A priest eating his portion at nightfall
Two people holding one cloak, each claiming it
A farmer leaving corners of a field
check.why: Bava Metzia begins with two people holding one garment. The Mishnah rules that they swear and divide it.

check.q: What are the two threads this course follows through the Talmud?
check.why: The course tracks how a sugya argues and what its ruling protects, argument and mercy.

check.q: What does 'Rashi explains the terms, the Tosafot compare the rule' show about the page?
choices: The layers disagree about which text is holy
Only the center of the page matters
Rashi and Tosafot wrote at the same time
Each layer works on the same question in its own way
check.why: The layers of the page each do a different job on the same passage: text, explanation, comparison.

review.q: Which text sits in the center of a standard Talmud page?
review.why: The center block holds the Mishnah and Gemara. Rashi and the Tosafot sit in the margins.

choices: The printer of the first complete Talmud
A commentator from Troyes, France, who lived 1040–1105
The editor of the Mishnah around 200
A rabbi of the Vilna press
review.why: Rashi, Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, lived in Troyes from 1040 to 1105 and wrote a commentary on almost the whole Talmud.

review.q: Where did Daniel Bomberg print the first complete Babylonian Talmud?
review.why: Bomberg's press was in Venice. He came from Antwerp. Vilna's edition came in the 1880s.

review.q: What is the main difference between the Mishnah's language and the Gemara's?
choices: The Mishnah is Aramaic; the Gemara is Hebrew
The Mishnah is mostly Hebrew; the Gemara is mostly Aramaic
review.why: The Mishnah was written mostly in Hebrew and the Gemara mostly in Aramaic, the spoken language of Babylonian Jews.

review.q: A student cites 'Avot 1:14.' What kind of text is that?
choices: A mishnah, cited by chapter and paragraph
A leaf of the Babylonian Talmud
A page of the Vilna Shas
review.why: Chapter-and-paragraph citations like 1:14 point to the Mishnah. Talmud pages are cited by leaf and side, like 2a.

review.q: Why is the Vilna Shas important?
choices: It was the first Talmud translated into English
It became the standard page that most later editions copied
It was the first printed Talmud
review.why: The Romm press's Vilna edition of 1880–86 fixed the look of the page that later editions reproduced.

review.q: What did the Tosafot add to the page?
choices: Questions comparing the passage with other pages of the Talmud
review.why: The Tosafot, written in the 1100s and 1200s, ask how a passage fits with others across the Talmud.

review.q: How many tractates does the Mishnah contain, in the standard count?
review.why: The Mishnah has 63 tractates in six orders. The Babylonian Gemara covers about 37 of them.
